The second is the amount of time and effort that all Members of the House, both in government and in opposition, have invested in legislation presently on the Order Paper at either committee stage, second reading or report stage.
The third reason is the importance of certain issues before the House and country which could not be foreseen when we laid out our agenda.
The fourth is the importance of the free trade initiative.
The fifth is the tactics of the Senate.
The sixth is the inflammatory comments and the delaying tactics of the Opposition.
First is our agenda. When we took office as a Government we decided to make some changes in accordance with the mandate given to us as a majority Government by the Canadian people. We sought to do and we sought to undo. We instituted a simplified approach to employment so that we could raise employment. We slashed spending. We slashed the deficit. We reduced the Public Service by some 15,000 people, mainly by attrition. We privatized Crown corporations. We enacted tougher laws dealing with prostitution, impaired driving, and the environment. We undid the National Energy Program which so unfairly crippled western Canada.
The list goes on and on. We deliberately set difficult goals for ourselves as a Government and we make no apologies for being ambitious because we believe Canada needs legislatures with ambition for their country.
This Parliament, the 33rd Parliament, has been one of the most productive in history to date. By coincidence, the 19741979 Parliament, which sat for 54 months, and the 1980-1984 Parliament, which sat for 51 months, both passed 177 Bills. This Parliament has passed 204 Bills in 44 months. In other words, if you deal with just the raw numbers, this Parliament has been 15 per cent more productive to date than previous Parliaments although it sat for much less time.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Then why sit in the summer?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I reiterate, we make no apologies for being ambitious as a Government.
Let us look at the amount of time and effort invested by Members of the House on all sides in the legislation currently before us. We wish to send the following legislation at the very least on to the Senate for consideration. We have Bills with respect to national parks, the proceeds of crime, the Official Languages Act, lobbyists' registration, the very important multiculturalism Bill, the privatization of Eldorado, or divestiture at any rate, amendments to the Canada Labour Code and the privatization of Air Canada. As well, we want to complete the reply to the Senate with respect to the amendments to the immigration Bill and the emergency refugee legislation.
The debate on those Bills has been spirited. We passed them at second reading. We have heard witnesses. There have been amendments in committee. There are amendments at report stage. I suggest we would all be remiss in our duty if we did not see that as much as possible of this legislation goes through to the conclusion of third reading and on to the Senate prior to the conclusion of this sitting. We suggest we owe that duty not only to Members of Parliament but to the witnesses and the people who sent us here.
The third item I referred to was those items which could not be foreseen when we laid out our agenda. I refer specifically to two things. First, the decision by the Supreme Court of Canada to declare the abortion law, which had been in existence since 1969, unconstitutional. The second matter was the Senate's decision to suggest amendments to the Meech Lake Accord, which requires the House to debate the matter for a second time and resolve once again the House's position. We feel it is our duty as elected representatives to debate those two items before we rise.
Fourth, we have the importance of the free trade initiative. The House knows, the country knows, that on January 2 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) signed an historic free trade agreement with the U.S. Legislation to implement that agreement had to be drafted and drafted properly. It had to be proceeded with at an appropriate time. We set about to draft that legislation, and whether or not Members opposite are in favour of the initiative, I think they would agree that, having taken that initiative, they would want that Bill to be drafted properly and as closely as possible to implement what was agreed between the parties. That is the issue before the House on Bill C-130. Does that Bill properly implement the agreement?
We believe the product is sound. My colleagues opposite disagree. That is fair. That is what democracy is all about, debating the issue, and we want to complete second reading of that legislation before we rise for the summer.
The fifth item to which I referred was the Senate. In completing our legislative agenda we have a further complication with which to deal, that is, the Senate. From 1980 to 1984 the Senate never had a sober second thought, at least not one that came back to the House of Commons. It was only in this Parliament that I and Members who were elected with me in 1979 found out how the reply from the Senate worked because it started to send legislation back to us for reconsideration. That never happened during the two previous long Parliaments when the sober second thoughts were presumably being delivered in another manner.
As well, the Senate discontinued what I respectfully suggest was a very useful procedure, that is, the prestudy of Bills. When the Conservatives came into government the Liberal dominated Senate suddenly decided not to prestudy Bills. Fortunately it has prestudied parts of the free trade issue and I
June 13, 1988

commend it for that, but I seriously ask why, if it wants to be part of this legislative process at the start, it did not continue that practice.
This very day on the Order Paper is consideration again by vote, at six o'clock, on the amendments to the Immigration Act. Also on the Order Paper, to follow up this particular motion, which we hope will go quickly, is the House's reply to the Senate's amendments to Bill C-84. I suggest to you, Madam Speaker, that our agenda has been disrupted by these very deliberate tactics of the Liberal dominated Senate.
Finally, we have to deal with the position of the Opposition with respect to the free trade legislation. I respect their position. I do not agree with it, but I respect their ability to take it and to put it forward. However, I question whether that opposition should be by way of delay rather than by debate.
I can recite a series of comments by the Opposition with respect to what it is going to do with the free trade legislation. To build the case I will quote the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) who said that his Party will try to stall passage of the Bill in the hope that public opinion or controversy within the Cabinet will force the Government to do the right thing.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg said "The real war is just beginning". The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) said:
Inevitably the government will cut off debate by invoking closure. But the Bill won't get out of the House of Commons until October, at the earliest.
The goal is not to stop the legislation cold, the goal is to force the government to pay such a high price that they eventually have got to see the logic of going for an election.
That is delay, that is not debate. Here is another quote from the same Member:
Our strategy is to try to slow down as much as possible the process of consideration of the Bill.
The strategy is not to win it by debate but to slow down the process of consideration.
There was a request for five days debate and the responsible comment of the House Leader of the New Democratic Party was: "Obviously we said no to that". The House Leader for the Liberal Party said: "We will fight the Government every step of the way".
When those comments are made we have to respond. We are prepared to debate and decide and the Opposition is prepared to delay and delay. When Canadians ask what the difference is between the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberals and New Democrats, that is the answer. We are prepared to debate and decide and the Opposition's only comment is to delay and delay.
When the House changed the rules in 1969 the Standing Orders were substantially revised by a motion before the House. That complete revamping of the rules took place by closure, closure, closure. That is what the Party which is now arguing against closure did.
Extension of Sittings
I want to read some quotes from some eminent personages- and I submit that these will bear scrutiny, that I am not taking them out of context-not with respect so much to closure but with respect to the rights of the minority. Here is a comment from Prime Minister Trudeau:
Every democratic assembly recognizes that issues will arise from time to time which the minority in all conscience cannot accept, which the minority in order to be true to its values must oppose vigorously and never concede. That is right and proper. It's one of the basis on which rests our democratic institution. But in a democracy the ballot box, not the filibuster, is the ultimate and appropriate technique of assessment as to the actions of the Opposition.
Mr. MacEachen said:
One cannot run a parliament without an ultimate sanction to prevent a minority preventing the majority from getting their way.
An excerpt from a book called Majority Rule by Elaine Spitz says:
In all electoral systems, what counts is open competitiveness and the consequent equal opportunity to make each vote count equally. Any organization of voting procedures that provides all with an equal opportunity to be heard in some significant way at some point in the process satisfies democratic principles.
Those are quotes from learned authorities. I looked for editorial comment and found the following from the Victoria Times-Colonist in the issue of May 26, 1988. It refers to the stalling tactics of the Opposition and says:
It's not good enough for the Opposition parties to justify such tactics on the grounds that the Mulroney government is selling off our sovereignty. No Canadian is naive enough to think that there won't be a downside to a free trade pact, but many believe the potential benefits far outweigh the disadvantages. The Grits and the NDP have yet to counter that argument convincingly, to say specifically what they would offer in place of free trade. Surely that is their opportunity and their constructive role in the weeks ahead.
If they just continue to play games they can expect scant public sympathy when the government finally invokes closure-in order to meet the Jan. 1, 1989 deadline for passing enabling legislation.
I submit that the Opposition has, quite rightfully, brought to the attention of the public its opposition to the free trade legislation. However, we do not believe that by extending the sittings, thereby extending the opportunity to debate that, we are in any way infringing on the responsibilities of the Opposition. We are giving them that opportunity.
That is the situation in which we find ourselves. We are an ambitious Government with a plan which has been well organized and is well under way. We are coping with unscheduled events and a planned and deliberate obstruction by a bragging Opposition and an appointed and anointed Liberal Senate.
The solution was two-fold. Number one, we put the motion on the Order Paper which allows us to complete our agenda. Number two, we wrote to the opposition Parties to see what could reasonably be completed before the House rose. I make no apologies, Madam Speaker. We included a very long list in writing the Opposition. I call it a "kitchen sink letter" and it was a kitchen sink letter. Everything but the kitchen sink was in the letter.

June 13, 1988
Extension of Sittings
The reply from the Liberal Party was very constructive. I have said that outside the House and say that on the record. My colleague, the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), delivered a very detailed and responsible response on behalf of the Liberal Party well in advance of the requested deadline. There are some differences of opinion, but we have an excellent starting point for negotiations.
By comparison, the response from the New Democratic Party was not what I had expected from a responsible Opposition. There was little or no effort to address the items on the Order Paper and I do not think it was responsible in any way whatsoever.
I therefore wrote another letter to the House Leader for the Liberal Party and sent a copy to the House Leader of the New Democratic Party. I cut down our list of legislation considerably by taking into account the legislation the Liberal Party said could be passed. Naturally, I added some five items which were not on the list of the Liberal Party. However, we got closer.
I went on to say that there may be certain items tabled in the near future on which we could make progress but it depends on negotiations between the Ministers and their spokespersons. In other words, since it is in the letter that has been made public, I state quite bluntly that it is up to Ministers and the spokespersons to work on items which are not on the Order Paper if they want to make progress.
Let me return to the free trade debate. It has been incorrectly suggested that we were prepared to allow five days only. While I did say five days, they were extended hours on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday which would result in some 27 hours of debating time, or nine days. I did not make any restriction to only five days, because if we are going to invoke closure or time allocation as the debate progresses, we will have to ask whether one more day or two more days after four days of debate will be sufficient.
The problem with negotiation in this business is that there must be a counter offer. There has been no counter offer on the free trade debate. There has been no suggestion that five days is not enough and the Opposition needs six. There has been no suggestion that they do not like the late hours on Thursday night and would rather sit late on Wednesday night. There has been no counter offer.
I went so far as to say that we would waive the eight hours rule so that after eight hours of debate on the substance and principle at second reading all speeches could be 20 minutes with 10 minutes for questions and comments. I suggested that we would waive that for the five days. There was no response. By the way, we are back to the eight-hour rule and thereafter every speech is 10 minutes.
I suggest to you, Madam Speaker, that we are open for this debate. I also suggest that while this is not a threat, all
Canadians will be looking to the free trade debate to see whether the Opposition wants to debate or delay during those days when it is called. In other words, Canadians will not call the exhibition of this morning, which was blown on procedural votes, a debate on free trade. They will call that delay. I suggest it will be difficult for the New Democratic Party, which pulled those stunts this morning, not the Liberal Party, to sustain that practice.
That is where we stand on this issue. I have laid out the reasons why the Government is taking this action. We are not trying to abuse the parliamentary calendar. It calls for a 10 week recess. We are prepared to work into that recess. While we are very close to coming together with the Liberal Party on this question, if the Opposition Parties speak against this motion as I expect they may, I want them to explain to Canadians exactly how they disagree with our proposition.
We are prepared and always have been prepared to discuss this matter. We do not expect the extension of this sitting to be protracted. I have suggested and I am still convinced that with the co-operation and the spirit of debate that our colleagues opposite want on the free trade agreement, we may well be able to finish what we are required to do by July 15 or even earlier.
In conclusion, I invite once again a serious review of our comments by the New Democratic Party in order that we may come together with the Liberal Party and settle this in the way that the people of Canada expect, that is as duly elected representatives with the interests of all their constituents at heart.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first let me say that we respect the judgment and the ruling of the Chair. While we are not happy that this motion has been declared allowable, it is out of respect for the Chair and for the rules of this institution that we have no choice and will enter debate on this motion. I think the Chair already knows our position with regard to the acceptability of the motion.
I know that the Minister of State (Mr. Lewis), the Deputy Government House Leader, has done his best to establish that what the Government is doing by introducing this motion is not an abuse of the rules of the House and an abuse of the Government's strength. The House will understand that I will be arguing just the opposite.
During the last election the Government promised to reform this place in order to allow the ordinary Member of Parliament a better say in what is done and in the decisions that are made. It is passing strange that the Government would come in with a steamroller and force the Opposition into a corner by using the might of its big majority to get its will.
Early in this Parliament when the Government tried to make people believe that it was fulfilling its election promise to reform the House, it appointed a committee on House reform chaired by the then Hon. Member for St. John's East, Mr. McGrath.
June 13, 1988



Mr. McGrath, now Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland, was given the mandate to reform the rules of the House and especially to try to give backbenchers a more important role.
So today we find ourselves in the situation where the Government is moving a motion that begins with the infamous words:
That, notwithstanding any Standing Order or practice of the House...
This is what Parliamentary reform means to the Conservative Party: to propose measures that begin by saying the Standing Orders do not apply.
If that is the reform the Government had in mind, it does not amount to much, really.

If the Minister of State wanted to make a good case, he should not have spoken. I will review what he has said just to prove my assertion.
At the conclusion of his speech he said that he does not believe the sitting this summer will be protracted and that in his opinion, everything might be finished by July 15. Why is there this blackmail to force the Opposition into thinking that we will have to sit until September 9 if it appears not to be true? Why state September 9 in the motion if the Minister sincerely believes everything will be finished by July 15? That is my first argument. If the Government wants to make a good case, it should ask the Minister to stay in his seat and not say anything.
The Minister began his speech by bragging that the Government has passed more legislation than previous Governments. Moments later, out of the other side of his mouth, he accused the Opposition of stalling tactics. That is a strange picture he is trying to paint for the Canadian public. We are supposedly stalling the business of the House, yet he likes to brag that the Government has passed more legislation than any previous government. I ask the House to try to reconcile that because I have had difficulty doing so myself.
The Minister told us about all the time invested by Members of Parliament into the various pieces of legislation. He has argued that some of these items must be completed. He fails to realize that the Government will have ample time to complete its program. If you believe that you will be canvassing in your riding during the summer, Madam Speaker, I suggest that will not happen because a government that is third in the polls will not call an election this summer. There will be ample time to sit in the fall and ample time to sit next spring before the Government can recuperate some of the support it needs to call an election. As as matter of fact, it would never call an election if it depended upon how Canadians feel about the Government. It will try to hang on forever. Fortunately, our Constitution puts an end to the term of any government after five years
Extension of Sittings
and the people of Canada will finish the job by putting an end to this Government.
The Government argues that it does not have enough time to complete the business in which it has so much time invested.

They will have time, Madam Speaker, they have at least another year until the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has the courage to call an election.
You will forgive me, Madam Speaker, if I spend too much time destroying the arguments of the Government House Leader. I have more things to say in reacting to what he said, but I am going to try to go quickly through his arguments and then give my own arguments. The Government House Leader talks about the importance of certain matters that could not be foreseen. All of a sudden, according to his argument, he wakes up one morning to a whole new set of circumstances he could not foresee and he has to react to it. For example, he talks about the Supreme Court decision to strike down the sections of the Criminal Code with respect to abortion. I know, of course, that the Government could not foresee that the Supreme Court would do that, but I will tell you, Madam Speaker, what I could not foresee and what no one in the country could foresee, and that is the reaction of the Government. It decided to shy away from the issue and present three options to the House of Commons. In that way, the ordinary back-bencher would not decide on legislation but would give the Government a sort of feeling of what the House thinks so that the Government can be taken off the hook and will not have to deal head on with that issue before the next election.
The Government on the hustings would also be able to say: "We had a debate on abortion in the House of Commons". That is what it is trying to do without making a decision and without bringing forward a Bill. The Government wants to negotiate. It is a very thorny issue if the Government wants to negotiate with the Opposition a Bill which is likely to receive support from all sides of the House. We are willing to talk, but we do not want the farce of bringing a three-headed monster into the House of Commons for the Government to hide behind so it can go on the hustings during the election campaign and say: "We dealt with that issue in the House of Commons", without making a decision. We were not able to foresee that the Government would do that.
The Government House Leader is now saying that the Government could not foresee having so little time for the free trade legislation. Well, the Government is late, and I will get into that. It will be part of my main speech. I want to show how late the Government is in bringing forward many of the items in the House of Commons and then trying to make everyone believe that it is because of the Opposition that it has to sit during the summer. I will demonstrate in a moment how the Government has dragged its feet on a number of items

June 13, 1988
Extension of Sittings
which it is now dropping on the Order Paper at the last minute. We would have to sit during the nights as well as the evenings during the summer to deal with all this legislation. It is hard enough for us to try to co-operate with such a Government but we cannot be in its offices doing its planning, God forbid.
I contend that the Minister of State had better not defend his case. Ele had better ask someone else to do it. The Government has had almost four years to pass its agenda through the House of Commons. There are several-and I will list them later-important pieces of legislation that the Government has delayed before bringing them to the House of Commons. Everyone in the country is now asking how come they are not yet passed. Everyone understands that between June 13 and the end of June, there is no possibility of passing all these items through the House of Commons, even if the Opposition was crazy enough to agree with all of the material, and we strongly disagree with some of these items.
A Government that cannot manage its business properly does not deserve to run the country. It deserves to be defeated in the next election, and this is exactly what will happen to this Government. The Government has a huge and distorted majority and it is trying to make the people of Canada believe that such a huge majority is powerless against what the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) would probably call us if he had the floor, a miniscule Opposition. We are a very small Opposition. Can the people of Canada believe that a handful of opposition Member can stop the Government, which has an unprecedented majority, to pass its legislation through the House of Commons? No one in the public would believe that. If it is true, the public must believe that we are facing a Government which is like the giant with clay feet.

A giant with feet of clay, a huge, apparently powerful giant that is unable to get its program passed because of a small handful of Opposition Members.

What can be more phoney than a Government telling us that it will sit all summer, and that is what the motion says, and then for the Minister to say he only needs until July 15? The Government proposes that we sit all summer and then denies the Opposition more than five days to discuss what is probably the most important piece of legislation ever introduced on the floor of the House of Commons since 1867, our first Parliament. I am talking, of course, of Bill C-130, the free trade legislation, which will affect the lives of us all. The Government tells us it needs the whole summer to discuss the business of the country, but it will only give us five days to discuss the most important piece of legislation that has ever been introduced in this House. It is ridiculous for the Government to try to have it both ways. I never thought government Members opposite would have the gall to try to get us to swallow that.

It will certainly take some swallowing, this story that we will be expected to sit all summer for two months, while we will only get five days of debate on the most important Bill this Government and many preceding governments ever tabled in the House of Commons.
Madam Speaker, what are the Government's motives for keeping the Opposition in the House all summer? I wondered about this last night at home, and I said to myself: They must have something in mind. I was watching tv and I saw the Prime Minister campaigning while he was in the riding of Joliette in fact today, he is in Alma, trying to salvage Mr. Bouchard's campaign, the Conservative candidate whose campaign is not doing well at all in Lac-Saint-Jean and then I thought I understood.
The Prime Minister may have this diabolical plan which is to spend the whole summer on a preliminary election campaign across the country, while his travelling expenses are still paid for by the taxpayers. He is acting in his capacity of Prime Minister, so the Conservative Party doesn't pay for the plane ticket which it would otherwise do in an election campaign. And in that case, travel expenses would be limited by the Canada Elections Act. For the time being, it doesn't cost the Conservative Party a cent for the Prime Minister to do some campaigning and distribute goodies across Canada. If we look at the Prime Minister's schedule, he is going from region to region, handing out big chunks of money, nearly $1 billion so far in terms of regional development for Quebec. And don't tell me that has no connection with the upcoming by-election!
So the concept is simple. It is to keep the Opposition in the House of Commons during the summer. The Government only needs one-third of the Conservative Caucus to maintain a majority in the House, and meanwhile, the election campaign can follow its course across the country, while the Opposition parties are stuck in the House of Commons. The taxpayers are paying for the Conservative election campaign, since they absorb the travelling expenses of the Prime Minister and his entourage, as well as the cost of the goodies the Prime Minister distributes at every stop and every airport. Maybe that is the idea!

The Government is doing it the wrong way this year. Last year, the Government played on the Canadian public its biggest hoax by saying there was an urgency in discussing Bills C-55 and C-84, the Immigration and Refugee Determination Bills. That was supposed to be a matter of great urgency. The Government wanted to sit in the summer, and it did. However, it did it the right way. It looked at the Standing Orders and it did not say, "notwithstanding any standing order". It did not say that. It used Standing Order 5, which I will not have to read to the Chair, which simply states that when the Government feels there is an emergency situation it can go to the Chair. The Government submits its reasons and the Chair makes a judgment.
June 13, 1988

That is exactly what Mr. Speaker did last summer. Mr. Speaker looked at the arguments presented by the Government. Mr. Speaker believed-I do not know if he would still believe it today-that there was a matter of sufficient urgency that he call the Members back. He interrupted the recess on August 10 and we started sitting again. We discussed these two Bills which, by the way, have not yet passed.
The Government did it the right way last summer. Why not do it the right way this summer? I will tell you why, Madam Speaker. It is because this summer, with the kind of phoney arguments that I have just demolished a few minutes ago, the arguments of the Minister, the Government dare not go to the Chair and ask the Speaker for permission to sit in the summer because it knows that it would be refused. If members of the Government were sure that their request would be accepted, it would be much easier than trying to circumvent the rules. That is the reason they are not doing it the right way this year.
If I were a Tory perhaps I would rather spend the summer in this place. First, some of the offices are air-conditioned. From what I hear in the ridings that I visit over the weekends, if I were a Tory I would not be too fond of going back to my riding. I know what the people are saying when they are talking about the Tory Party. They prefer to be sitting here in the safety of their seats in the House of Commons where no one can kick them in the shins. Pages and all the Officers of the House of Commons are very polite people, they do not kick them. But when they go back to their ridings I know the kind of hell they get from their electors. Maybe the reason they want to spend the summer here is that they dare not spend the summer in their ridings.
I would now like to review some of the items that we have before us in terms of legislation. Let us see if the Government is sincere when it says that it needs the summer to complete his agenda. For example, there is a very much needed amendment to the National Housing Act. We advised the Government that we were ready to co-operate with respect to this measure. On February 12 the Government introduced legislation with respect to this matter. It is one thing to introduce a piece of legislation and an entirely different thing to bring it up for debate and to pass it in the House. My question is what has the Government done since February 12 with respect to the National Housing Act? Will the Government blame the Opposition? No. It has not brought it forward for debate. It is on the Order Paper but it does not move it ahead.
Do you want something more interesting, Madam Speaker? On February 24 with great fanfare the Government tabled conflict of interest legislation. It was supposed to protect the Government and the people of Canada from dishonesty in government. The Government took a big PR move by introducing it. I know that you follow the business of the House very closely, Madam Speaker. Can you tell me one day after February 24 when Your Honour has seen this measure
Extension of Sittings
debated in the House? Of course you cannot because there has been no debate.

Was the conflict of interest legislation tabled by the Government on February 24 just a public relations stunt, to give Canadians the impression that stricter legislation would stop Conservative ministers from putting the Government in an awkward position? Was it supposed to make Canadians believe stricter legislation would mean fewer violations? All I can say is that since then, the Bill was not brought back to the House for debate, and it wasn't the Opposition that prevented them from doing so. And this is one of the Government's priorities before the next election. Too bad. Until they bring the Bill before the House for debate, I can't pass it. Tabling the Bill is not my prerogative nor is it my Party's prerogative.
Take Bill C-93, for instance. The multiculturalism Bill was reported back to the House from committee on May 19. That was almost a month ago. The Bill would pass the House of Commons easily, but here again, the Government has not brought the Bill back for debate.
Another Bill, Bill C-82, was reported back to the House by its Legislative Committee. It is another piece of legislation that deals with honesty and openness in government. This was the Bill on lobbying, a Bill that met with no opposition or filibustering-another cornerstone of the Government's "squeaky clean" campaign. I wonder what Mr. Clean is thinking up in Lac-Saint-Jean, the man who was appointed to be the watchdog of the Government's integrity and who has now finally realized .. he may not be required to listen to what we are saying here in the House, but I am sure someone is going to report that I said the lobby Bill does not seem to be a priority for the Government. Just as, since February 24, conflict of interest legislation does not seem to have been a priority.
Take tax reform. They will say it is important for the House to sit all summer because it has to pass the tax reform Bill which has a high priority. If it has such a high priority, Madam Speaker, it should be brought before the House. Today is June 13, and the Bill first appeared on the Order Paper-I checked this morning-on June 10. That was last Friday which is certainly not that long ago. That has not been brought up for debate yet. They simply gave notice because they realize that they look stupid; people say that they are not serious about tax reform. So they put a notice in the Order Paper, but we have not had five minutes of debate on it. They would have us believe that it is our fault for all the items I have listed for you. They cannot blame the Opposition-they are the ones who are not moving to start the debate on those items.
On abortion, on May 20, they tabled the ridiculous threeheaded monster, with three options, in the Order Paper. But despite that, they did not begin the debate. That was almost a month ago.

June 13, 1988
Extension of Sittings
As for Bill C-130 on free trade, it had been promised-those who follow the debates here, who follow question period, know that the Government had promised it for the first week in March. Look, it is now June 13 and we are not yet debating it. It was only tabled on May 24, two months late. I tell you that if they took two months more to draft the Bill, they cannot blame it all on the Opposition.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: They have to get their act together on the other side.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: That's right, because it may take them time to reach an agreement. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) may be right. Sometimes they can't reach agreement in that party. Anyway, they took a lot of time to come up with Bill C-130. Today, they blame the Opposition for delaying its passage and furthermore, they tell us that we will have just five days to talk about it. We will have to sit two more months in the summer, but have only five days for that Bill. How come we will have only five days to discuss it, while the Government took months to write it?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: That's dictatorship.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
It's dictatorship, as the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) says.
Listen, I'll give you more examples: Bill C-128 establishing the Department of Industry, Science and Technology was promised last June. Do you know how long ago that Bill was tabled, Madam Speaker? It was tabled yesterday. Look at the Order Paper and you will see that. And I suppose they will tell us that the Opposition is preventing the Government from working.

Let us look at the Government's long awaited film policy. It took it a long time to think this one out. It had to consult a great many people.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: They had to consult Reagan in the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
They had to get more than that. They had to get their instructions from Jack Valenti, the czar of the U.S. film industry. Once they got their marching orders from him, on June 8, 1988, they tabled a piece of legislation. Two years ago we were pressing the Government to bring in a film policy. Everyone in Canada knows that we need a film policy. Everyone knows we have to take care of who distributes the films shown in Canadian cinemas. It took the Government two years to deliver this one on June 8, five days ago, Madam Speaker. Therefore, do not expect this piece of legislation to be passed by tonight. The Government has not brought it forward for debate yet.
Where is Meech Lake? It came back from the Senate and the Government is supposed to discuss it in the House. It came
back from the Senate and it has been sitting on the Order Paper since May 19. In six days it will be one month. Where is the Meech Lake Accord? On this side of the House we do not intend to procrastinate the debate on the Meech Lake Accord. That debate has already taken place in the House. All we want to do is deal with it in an expeditious fashion. What is the Government doing? Nothing. I presume the Government would prefer to call an election with this not passed and attempt to blame it on the Opposition.
Where is the child care policy? It is even worse in this area because I cannot point to the Order Paper, Madam Speaker, and show you a Bill. There is nothing on the Order Paper. For years the Government has been saying that it will have a child care policy.

... a child care policy. There is nothing on the Order Paper, they have not even tabled a Bill and they would have us believe that they want to pass it during the summer, I suppose! They have not even brought their Bills forward.

In conclusion, Madam Speaker, we want to co-operate with the Government in providing extra hours to attempt to deal with the unfinished business of the Government, even if we have to hold our nose when we vote against some of the pieces of legislation. We would be willing to extend the hours. Standing Order 10 allows for that. Once again I will bring it to the attention of the Government, because it will give them a recipe to do things in the proper manner. The heading is "Extension of Sitting Hours" and Standing Order 10(1) reads as follows:
On the tenth sitting day preceding June 30 a motion to extend the hours of
sitting to a specific hour during the last ten sitting days may be proposed,
without notice, by any Member during Routine Proceedings.
In Standing Order 10(2) the question is put in the following manner:
Not more than two hours after the commencement of proceedings thereon,
the Speaker shall put every question necessary to dispose of the said motion.
If the Government wants more hours, it could use Standing Order 10. It does not have to go around the Standing Orders and write a motion which states:
That, notwithstanding any Standing Order or practice of the House ...
All the Government has to do is use Standing Order 10. If that was done, we would be ready to co-operate.
In order to help the Government do it in the proper manner, I would like to propose an amendment which will have the effect of simply offering the opportunity to the Government to go the route of Standing Order 10 which I just quoted. In this manner we could co-operate with the Government, give it more hours, which is what the Government wants, and we would not have to violate the whole book by saying: "Notwithstanding any Standing Orders ... ",
June 13, 1988

I move, seconded by my hon. colleague for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier):
That the motion be amended by deleting the following:
"Friday, September 9, 1988, the House will meet on the days and at the
times specified in Standing Order 3, but not on August 1;
That, during such period"
and by substituting the following therefor:
"Thursday, June 30, 1988".
Therefore, the hours will be extended, but not until September 9. The hours will be extended until the end of the month, like the Standing Orders call for.

That would be the honest way for the Government to proceed, and that is why we are suggesting to go back to Standing Order 10, which allows not only the Party in power to extend the hours of sitting, but also Opposition Members of back-benchers. The Order states that the motion "may be proposed by any Member". It doesn't have to be a Minister. This means that any Member could rise and propose that we give the government more time to debate. A Minister can do it. I myself have just done it on the Opposition's behalf. I have just proposed to extend the hours of sitting, but in a reasonable way, without suspending our Standing Orders but by making use of a Standing Order established for that purpose, namely to allow for an extension of sitting hours so as to have more time to debate questions before the House.
That is the kind of co-operation we are ready to give the Government so that bills which it deems important can be passed. I am not saying that we will vote favourably on all these Bills, since there are some we don't like, but at least, the Government will have more time for the adoption of its legislative program. And we believe that is what must be done. We are ready to cooperate, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today there is a certain sense of deja vu in the House of Commons. Despite the sunny skies above there has been a dark cloud hanging over Parliament Hill for the last hour or so.
It reminds me of October 23, 1980, when the Progressive Conservatives in Opposition decided that they had had enough of democracy; they had had enough of the Parliament of Canada as had been practised for decades and decades. They disagreed with the Speaker's decision, and rather than accept the decision of the Speaker, some of the Members in the House rushed up to the Speaker's chair screaming and yelling at the tops of their voices: "Stop it!". They were screaming and
Extension of Sittings
yelling in front of the Speaker. There are some Ministers present today who actually did that on October 23, 1980. They stormed the Chair demanding their rights to be heard despite the fascist totalitarian motion to cut off debate.
In 1980 the Conservatives called the Liberals fascist and totalitarian because the Liberals had decided to limit debate. Had the Government of the day decided to limit debate after a handful of speakers? No. There were 98 Conservatives who spoke in that debate. They stood up and made comments on the constitutional amendment. Then the Government of the day said 98 interventions on behalf of the Opposition was sufficient and it was going to limit debate and bring in closure. The Conservatives of the day went absolutely mad. I was present. It was one of the saddest days that parliamentarians have ever had. The Conservatives screamed and demanded that they be heard.
Now the tables are turned. Now the Conservatives are sitting on the government side and they have decided, because they have this huge majority, that they are now going to take this rule book of Standing Orders and throw it out of the window. That is it, throw it out the window. They are saying: "We know best. Big Brother Government knows what is best for Parliament, the Speaker does not". The Government is saying that you, Madam Speaker, do not know what is best for this House, that the Speaker of the House of Commons is not in a position to recall Parliament if he or she considers it necessary.
No, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has decided on behalf of Parliament, forget the Liberals, the New Democrats and the Independents. The Conservatives have the majority and therefore can do anything they want. They do not have to play by these rules that have developed over decades. They do not have to accept these rules which were developed after months and months of study between all the Parties and were adopted by unanimous consent of the House. No, they are saying: "We are going to throw them out, we are going to rip out the pages of this rule book and we are going to impose our own rules". That is like the Edmonton Oilers saying: "We are going to change the rules of hockey. We are going to throw out all the rules and introduce our own." Do you know when the Government last suspended the rules to meet its own political agenda, Madam Speaker? It was in 1883. Not since 1883 has a Government suspended the rules to facilitate its own political agenda.
We are now seeing a whole new approach to democracy in Canada. We do not like the rules, so we make our own. We do not like the way the Speaker might rule, so we will ignore the Speaker. The Government will use its majority. The sounds of jackboots are banging around Parliament Hill these days as the Conservatives impose the will of their majority against parliamentary tradition.

June 13, 1988
Extension of Sittings
Forget parliamentary tradition, forget parliamentary practices, forget parliamentary regulations, forget the Standing Orders. Big brother Mulroney knows best what is good for the House of Commons. We reject that.
We will as concerned parliamentarians accept the ruling of the Speaker. However, this country has now started on a new path thanks to the Conservative majority in the House. Whatever the Government decides it does not want, it will change. It will simply suspend the orders.
What will come next? I wonder if the Conservatives will not change Standing Order 2 which provides for the election of the Speaker and say: "Why don't we simply impose on the House of Commons the Speaker we want?". Why not do that next? If they can suspend the rules for their own purposes, why should we have Question Period? Question Period is messy. Opposition and New Democratic Party Members pose difficult questions every day, so let's do away with that. Let's suspend Question Period and Statements Pursuant to Standing Order 21. Let's do away with Private Members' Hour. If we let Government Members get away with the suspension of this Standing Order, why would they not introduce other suspensions of rules that are aggravating and disrupt their parliamentary agenda?
Today's motion tells me that I am incompetent and that the Deputy House Leader of the Government is incompetent. He says that although we have been here for 11 months, the Government is not able to manage its parliamentary agenda or its timetable, so it is incompetent. It cannot follow the parliamentary calendar. The Deputy Government House Leader is indicating that in spite of sitting here for 11 months, we cannot handle the work of the House of Commons. We need more time.
A person cannot walk down two sides of the road at the same time nor talk out of both sides of his or her mouth at the same time, with one exception and that is the Deputy House Leader of the Government. He is able to do that. On one hand, he is saying: "Look at our impressive record. We have passed more legislation in this Parliament than any Parliament in recent time". At the same time, he is saying: "Those tough Opposition and NDP people are holding us up. They are holding up our ability to do the business of the House". He cannot have it both ways. He cannot brag about the tremendous success he has had in moving business through the House of Commons at the same time that he is saying that the Opposition is not allowing the Government to get on with the business of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Let's admit it, you want to go home.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: A Tory yells out that we all want to go home. They can go to Victoria and sit around their pools. As long as we are fighting this trade deal, the New Democrats are prepared to fight it today, tonight, next week, in the month of July and in the month of August. We will fight it as long as it takes to force the Government into an election.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Why are we doing this? Why are New Democrats frustrating the Government's efforts to introduce and pass the trade legislation? Do Hon. Members remember the view of the Prime Minister on free trade back in 1983? He was against free trade with the United States. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was against free trade with the United States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) was against free trade with the United States. The only leadership candidate for the Conservative Party who was in favour of it was Peter Pocklington. He was the only one who was advocating free trade.
In 1984, there was a general election. How many times did the Prime Minister mention free trade during the general election campaign? Not one single time, not a single phrase was uttered during the entire election about free trade. Then what did he do? On January 2, the Prime Minister of Canada, with his good buddy Ronald Reagan, signed Canada in to this trade deal.
We believe in democracy. We New Democrats do not rush up and challenge the Speaker's ruling. We do not start screaming, yelling and stopping the Speaker from talking as the Conservatives did in October of 1980. We believe in democracy and that is why we are saying that the Government should call an election. Let's go to the people of Canada and let them decide.
We are prepared to work as long as it takes to force the Government to come to its democratic senses and call an election, but I do not think it will. It thinks it has the bit between its teeth now. It thinks it can do whatever it wants now.
Think of the abortion resolution, Madam Speaker. Rather than showing leadership and bringing in a Bill that would be debated in the House of Commons as usual, it brought in a three headed monster. If some Hon. Members want to support abortion on demand, there is a motion for them. If some want to support no abortion at all, there is a motion for them. If some want a compromise in the middle, there will be a motion for them. What kind of decision-making is that? What kind of leadership is that?
To move that kind of a motion, the Government has to suspend the rules of the House of Commons, but it will do it. It has no hesitation in doing that. It has no concern for something called the traditions of this House, something called the practices of Parliament, something called rules and regulations, something called Standing Orders. All those things are a nuisance to the Conservatives in the House. Set them aside, suspend the rules, suspend the traditions, let the Government do what it wants because it has the numbers. It has the majority and it can do anything it wants.
We have just begun. The New Democrats have just begun to remind the Conservatives that that kind of arrogance has no
June 13, 1988

place in a parliamentary democracy. We have just begun to fight.
The Government says it has important legislation to introduce. Where is the child care legislation? The Government says it has child care legislation that the Opposition is holding up. Have you seen the child care legislation, Madam Speaker? No, you have not. It has not been introduced, so how can we be holding up legislation that has not even been introduced in the House of Commons? That is just one Bill. I could list a whole number of pieces of legislation that the Government wants passed expeditiously and quickly, preferably without debate. However, we have not even seen that legislation. It has not been introduced in the House of Commons.
I remember the Throne Speech of 1984. The Government said that one of its priorities was to introduce legislation regarding child care. We waited for the fall of 1984, we waited all of 1985, we waited all of 1986 and all of 1987. It is now well into 1988 and we still have not seen a single page of legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Slow workers.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that they are slow workers. This is government in reverse.
Since this Opposition does not want to co-operate on the trade deal, the solution now is to force the Opposition into it. The Government is going to exhaust the Opposition into it because it is a very small group. There are only 33 New Democrats and 40 Liberals-

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Thirty-three too many.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I know there are too many of us as far as the Conservatives are concerned. They do not want any opposition. Their ideal world is to have a dictatorship, just one party. That is their ideal.
There is a new wave occurring in Canada. This is not a one-Party system. There is an opposition and we do not plan to cooperate on the trade deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Or on anything else.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
On anything else, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) says. He is wrong. Last Thursday we demonstrated that. Five Bills were introduced on Indian concerns. We said that we would pass them expeditiously because the legislation was good. We co-operated 100 per cent. For one of the very first times all five Bills moved through the House of Commons in a single day. If the Government brings forward good legislation, we will pass it expeditiously. If the Government brings in assistance to the farmers, that legislation will go through here like you have never seen it before, like greased lightning, Mr. Speaker. If the
Extension of Sittings
Government brings in legislation on flow-through shares, again it will go like greased lightning through this place, but not legislation to implement the trade deal that will redirect not only the economic policies of this country but the social, cultural and the political policies of this country. In other words, the Government wants to turn this country into a fifty-first state, and we say no.
Let me say why we felt it was appropriate that we follow the parliamentary calendar. After months and months of study, Members of the House of Commons unanimously agreed it would be useful and it would make a great deal of sense if we established a parliamentary calendar. We would sit as a Parliament for 10 months of the year and then for July and August we would break from the House of Commons so that we could go back to our constituencies and work. Most of us have made plans during July and August in our constituencies. Call them constituency tours, meetings, or special gatherings with groups. The parliamentary calendar said that was when we could do that, and we agreed. Even the Conservatives agreed to the parliamentary calendar. We made plans. We felt it was important that Members of Parliament have some time to spend with their families. This might not be a priority for the Conservatives but for some of us it is. Spending time with our families and our constituents is important. We all agreed unanimously that for the months of July and August we would do just that. All of a sudden, the Conservatives said: "We don't like this idea. We don't like the idea of Members going home to their constituents and conducting tours".

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: "We are going to force you to sit during the summer months". Again, that goes against the unanimous decision made as a Parliament. The Minister in his comments indicated that the Government is very big hearted and has decided that for the trade legislation, which the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) said is the most important legislation introduced since the Second World War, there will be five days of debate. Only five days debate on the trade legislation. We have three or four days debate on routine tax Bills but on the largest piece of legislation with its implications not only for this generation of Canadians but for generations afterwards the Government said it will allow five days debate, do we agree.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Five days with some extension.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: To be fair, five days with some extension and a few hours into the evening. Remember, Madam Speaker, this proposal comes from a Party which gave 98 speeches on the Constitution and then, if you like, threatened the Speaker in the chair because its Members felt that their speaking rights were being terminated. The Conservatives said they would be generous and allow five days of debate for all 282 Members of the House of Commons.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
It is nine days at second reading.

June 13, 1988
Extension of Sittings

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
It is appalling, undemocratic and it is certainly unparliamentary. We rejected strongly such a ludicrous request.
I want to say that the Government has not seen what a filibuster is all about. The Government might want to change the standing rules to suit its purposes. If the Conservatives don't like Question Period, I guess they will say Question Period is too aggravating. We may hear such things as: "We do not like the Standing Orders so we will change that as well". Because private Members are allowed 15 minutes a day to make statements about constituencies' concerns, I guess that too will be done away with. I can see the next change to the Standing Orders will be the suspension of the 10 months' sitting. The Conservatives may want only one or two weeks to bring in one big omnibus Bill and that will take care of the business of Canada.
That is not the kind of country we want. That is not the kind of country for which the legionnaires, 4,000 of them who are meeting in Ottawa today, fought. That is not the kind of government which those 4,000 legionnaires went overseas to defend. For those legionnaires in the gallery at the moment, I suspect they are thinking right now that here is a government prepared to rip up those freedoms for which they fought and is prepared to set aside the rules, traditions and fundamental practices of democracy for which we were prepared to die. That is what we are seeing today.
We are seeing a very negative spectacle when it comes to a democratic free country. That is why we say this particular motion is wrong. We accept the Speaker's decision. We must accept it. We will not rush the Chair or cause havoc in the House of Commons because we do not like the ruling. We will accept that. We have now moved the course of this place in a totally different direction where with a majority you can do anything you want. If you have the majority you can change any Standing Order you want, permanently, or simply suspend it. You can break any rule. You can throw out any tradition.
As I say, this is a dark day for our Parliament. It reminds me of the day back in October, 1980. It is not the kind of Canada most of us want to see. It is not the kind of Canada our constituents want to see. Our constituents have made it clear in every possible way that they want to see an election on this trade deal. They want an opportunity to participate in whether or not we should sign away our future to the United States. Canadians want to make that decision. In a democratic society, Madam Speaker, in a Parliament that says it believes in the democratic traditions, we ought to give the people of Canada that right and that opportunity. To do that, if necessary, we in the New Democratic Party, will do everything we can in our power to use the legitimate rules of Parliament to encourage the Government to live up to the free democratic traditions and principles that Canadians love and enjoy.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Questions and comments.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I wish to commend my colleague for an excellent address on the question of suspending the Standing Orders. It seems to me that in a parliamentary democracy it is the accepted practices, built up over the sittings and the years, that really constitute the essence of our democracy. It seems to me that when the Government suspends the rules of the House it sets a very dangerous precedent. As I think my House Leader pointed out, if you start suspending the rules today on these particular issues, what comes next? You begin to suspend them with respect to Question Period, with respect to how Bills are moved through the House, indeed how the House governs itself.
What the Government is doing today is setting a precedent. What will stop some future Government from using that precedent and doing exactly the same thing? Once the Government, any Government, starts down that road, future Governments will use it as a precedent to be employed in other situations. Once you start down that road, it continues and continues and our Standing Orders, the rules under which we govern ourselves, are no longer meaningful. It is the precedent that it sets that creates a new standard, a new way in which Governments can deal with the Opposition and subvert Parliament. My House Leader said that not since the 1800s has a Government used this ploy of suspending the Standing Orders. We were fortunate that it did not become a practice.
Surely what the Government is doing today is demonstrating that even with its massive majority it cannot set its agenda and pass its legislation within the established rules. It must therefore suspend those rules. Surely this is a very dangerous precedent. Surely Conservative Members who cherish the traditions of the British parliamentary procedure must feel extremely uncomfortable with what their own Government is doing.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to respond to my hon. colleague who of course raises the fundamental question before us today, where does this take us? What is the next step?

June 13, 1988
It was back in March of 1883 that the Standing Orders were last suspended and now they are being suspended again.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: A Tory Government then, too.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: It was a Conservative Government, was it not?

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: I believe it was.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: I guess we should not be puzzled by these antics, then. First we had the suspension of the rules in 1883. I referred earlier to the storming of the Chair by the Conservatives during the constitutional debate. I failed to mention that in 1982 it was again the Conservatives who shut down Parliament for more than two weeks.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Because of the NEP.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: It does not matter why. In other words, the ends justify the means? The Conservatives say they have a right to do that. I like that. They say they were angry at the NEP. The Liberals brought that in, they did not like it, so they can shut down Parliament. That is fine. Because they do not like legislation it is all right for them to shut down Parliament. Because the NDP and Liberals are concerned about the trade deal we cannot have more than a five day debate. What nonsense, absolute nonsense.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Louder.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
It is typical coming from a Conservative, though. They felt they could close down the Parliament of Canada for a couple of weeks. That was all right because they were angry at the Government.
They were angry at the Speaker so they could storm the Chair and make a mockery out of that position. Harvie Andre was there, leading the pack, screaming and yelling. Total abuse of the parliamentary system. So why are we puzzled today when the Conservatives once again act on their view of democracy which we call tyranny, a dictatorship.
Our Parliament is based on the Mother of Parliaments. I thought all of us had a deep respect for the parliamentary system where we recognized the role of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: We are following tradition.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I know the Minister dislikes opposition Parties. Maybe he should go to the Soviet Union or Chile. He will feel more comfortable in one of those countries.
There are still Members in this House who cherish the idea of Parliament. There are still Members who cherish the ideal of a Government and opposition Party. The opposition Parties are here to keep the Government honest. To do that, you need to have a Parliament in session and working. The Conservatives who said in 1982 that they were going to shut down Parliament are the same Conservatives who are saying today that they are going to bring in closure and time allocation. They do not want debate on this. They do not like the Standing
Extension of Sittings
Orders and they are prepared to suspend them for now. The last time the Government did that was in March of 1883.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: I remember it well.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: You look like you do.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Here we go again.
My colleague's second question was what is the alternative to the Government introducing this motion? The alternative is the Chair. You will know that Standing Order No. 5 gives the Speaker authority to recall Parliament whenever he or she decides it is in the best interests of the country to do that. If we were to recess as the calendar says we ought to, on June 30, and on July 5 or July 10 the Government was able to make a case that it was in the nation's interest that the Speaker recall Parliament, you have the right to do that. We have unanimously given you that right. We say we trust the Speaker because the Speaker represents all Members of the House. The Speaker is elected by all Members. You represent the Government, the Opposition and the independent Members. We put that faith in you and in your position. Yet the Government has ripped that out of your hands. It knows best. It is Big Brother. It does not have to listen to the Speaker or convince the Speaker to sit during the summer months.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext: Very dangerous.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
